title: More Than Two Outcomes with elif
content:
What problem does this solve?
Real decisions rarely have only two paths. A hero might be healthy, wounded, or critical — three different messages, one health value. elif lets you chain conditions so Python picks the first match and skips the rest.

Basic syntax
  if health > 50:
      print("healthy")
  elif health > 0:
      print("wounded")
  else:
      print("critical")

What actually happens
Python checks conditions top to bottom. The first true block runs, then the entire chain is finished — no other branch runs. At health 50, health > 50 is false, so Python tries elif health > 0, which is true, and prints wounded.

When this is useful
Use elif when several ranges or tiers are possible and exactly one outcome should happen.
concepts: elif adds more branches between if and else
Only the first true condition runs
Order matters — put more specific checks before general ones

examples.title: Health tier labels
examples.explanation: 35 is not above 50, but it is above 0, so wounded is chosen.

examples.title: Gold purchase tiers
examples.explanation: 12 satisfies the elif branch — enough for a potion, not armor.

common_mistakes: Writing else if instead of elif — Python uses elif as one keyword
Using several separate if statements when only one outcome should print
Putting a broad condition before a specific one so the specific branch never runs

exercises.title: Predict the tier at a boundary
exercises.prompt:
Mira's health is exactly 50. Trace the elif chain top to bottom before you answer.

Decide your answer, then click Check — Run does not grade predictions.
exercises.failure_message: 50 is not greater than 50, so the first branch is skipped. Which elif condition is true next?
hints: Work top to bottom: is health > 50 true when health is 50?
When the first condition is false, Python tries the elif.
50 is greater than 0, so the elif branch runs.

exercises.title: Complete the purchase chain
exercises.prompt:
Fill in the missing condition so gold of 15 prints buy potion (not buy armor and not save up).

Replace None with the correct comparison.
hints: The elif should catch prices between armor and broke.
A potion costs at least 10 gold.
Use gold >= 10 so 15 takes the potion branch.

tests.message: Keep the if / elif / else structure.

exercises.title: Label wound severity
exercises.prompt:
Write wound_label(health) that returns a string:
- "healthy" when health is greater than 50
- "wounded" when health is greater than 0 (but not healthy)
- "critical" when health is 0 or below

Return the label — do not print it. Use if / elif / else.
exercises.success_message: You chose exactly one tier for every health value using an elif chain — the same pattern you will reuse for gates and purchases.
hints: Check the healthiest tier first: health > 50.
The middle tier catches anything above 0 that is not healthy.
Use else for zero or negative health.
Return a string from each branch; only one branch should run per call.

tests.message: When health is 80, the healthy tier should run.
When health is exactly 50, the healthy check fails — wounded should run.
Zero health should be critical, not wounded.
Negative health should still be critical.
Generalize the tiers — health 17 should still be wounded.
Mid-range health like 33 should return wounded, not a hardcoded table entry.

exercises.title: One label or many?
choices: Keep three separate if statements — check every condition
Use one if / elif / else chain so the first match wins
exercises.success_message: Right — elif stops after the first true branch. Separate ifs with return can work too; the bug appears when multiple blocks can run (such as several prints).
exercises.failure_message: Separate if blocks are independent. When several conditions are true, several blocks can run. A chain picks exactly one path.
hints: Ask what happens at health 80 with three separate if checks.
After one branch runs in a chain, the rest are skipped.
